title: Chromatin Architecture
description: From the nucleosome to topologically associating domains

concepts.title: The Nucleosome and the 11 nm Fiber
concepts.contentHtml:
The fundamental unit of chromatin is the nucleosome: 147 base pairs of DNA wrapped 1.65 turns around a histone octamer (two copies each of H2A, H2B, H3, H4). The crystal structure (Luger et al., 1997) revealed how DNA contacts arginines on the histone surface every ~10 bp where the minor groove faces inward. Linker DNA between nucleosomes is bound by histone H1, the linker histone, which clamps DNA at entry/exit and stabilises higher-order folding.

This produces the 11 nm "beads-on-a-string" fiber, the canonical electron-microscopy image of decompacted chromatin. Variant histones diversify the array: H2A.Z flanks active promoters and destabilises nucleosomes, H3.3 marks active transcription sites and is deposited replication-independently by HIRA, and CENP-A replaces H3 specifically at centromeres to template kinetochore assembly.

Nucleosome positioning is not random. ATP-dependent remodelers (SWI/SNF, ISWI, CHD, INO80 families) slide, evict, or exchange histones to expose or occlude binding sites. A nucleosome-depleted region (NDR) at active promoters and well-positioned +1 nucleosomes downstream are universal features detectable in MNase-seq.

concepts.title: From 30 nm Fiber to Loops and Compartments
concepts.contentHtml:
The classical model proposed a 30 nm fiber formed by zigzag or solenoid folding of the 11 nm array. In vitro, reconstituted arrays under physiological salt do form 30 nm structures, but cryo-EM tomography of intact nuclei (Ou et al., 2017) finds chromatin instead exists as a disordered 5–24 nm polymer melt. The 30 nm fiber appears to be a refolded artefact rather than the dominant in vivo state.

At larger scales, Hi-C contact maps reveal a hierarchy. The genome partitions into A/B compartments (active euchromatin / repressive heterochromatin, ~5 Mb) and within them into topologically associating domains (TADs) of ~100 kb–1 Mb where contacts are enriched.

TADs are organised by cohesin loop extrusion: the cohesin ring threads chromatin until it encounters convergent CTCF binding sites, producing the corner-peak loops visible in Hi-C. Acute auxin-induced degradation of cohesin (Rao et al., 2017) abolishes TADs within hours but leaves compartments intact, demonstrating the two are mechanistically distinct.

concepts.title: Euchromatin, Heterochromatin, and Phase Separation
concepts.contentHtml:
Euchromatin is gene-dense, accessible, and replicates early. Constitutive heterochromatin (centromeres, pericentric satellites, telomeres) is marked by H3K9me2/3, bound by HP1 proteins, and is silent and late-replicating. Facultative heterochromatin (the inactive X, developmentally repressed loci) is marked by Polycomb-deposited H3K27me3 and is reversible.

Heterochromatin is increasingly understood as a biomolecular condensate formed by liquid–liquid phase separation. HP1α dimerises, oligomerises, and phase-separates in vitro at physiological concentrations (Larson et al., 2017; Strom et al., 2017). The condensate concentrates silencing factors and excludes RNA polymerase II, providing a physical mechanism for spreading and compartmentalisation that pure pairwise binding cannot explain.

Lamin-associated domains (LADs) tether ~40% of the genome to the nuclear lamina via LBR and emerin. LADs are gene-poor, late-replicating, and enriched in repressive marks. Detachment from the lamina during differentiation can derepress lineage-specific genes, illustrating that 3D position itself is a regulatory layer.

title: DNA Methylation
description: CpG islands, the DNMT family, TET-mediated demethylation, and methylome readout

concepts.title: CpG Dinucleotides and CpG Islands
concepts.contentHtml:
In mammalian genomes, cytosine methylation occurs almost exclusively at CpG dinucleotides — a cytosine followed by a guanine on the same strand. About 70–80% of all CpGs are methylated. Because 5-methylcytosine spontaneously deaminates to thymine (whereas unmethylated C deaminates to uracil and is repaired), CpG sites have been depleted across evolution: the genome contains only ~20% of the CpGs predicted by base composition alone.

The exception is the CpG island: a region typically 200 bp–2 kb with elevated CG content (>50%) and observed/expected CpG ratio >0.6. About 70% of human gene promoters overlap a CpG island, and these islands are usually unmethylated regardless of expression. Methylation of a promoter CpG island is a strong silencing signal — used by the cell at imprinted genes and on the inactive X, and hijacked by tumours to silence tumour suppressors such as MLH1, CDKN2A, and BRCA1.

Beyond promoters, gene bodies of actively transcribed genes are paradoxically highly methylated. This gene-body methylation suppresses cryptic intragenic promoters and influences alternative splicing rather than silencing the gene.

concepts.title: Writers: DNMT1 vs DNMT3A/B
concepts.contentHtml:
Three catalytically active DNA methyltransferases write 5mC. DNMT1 is the maintenance methyltransferase: it is recruited to replication forks via UHRF1, which recognises hemimethylated CpGs (methylated parental strand, unmethylated daughter). DNMT1 then copies the parental methylation pattern onto the new strand, propagating the methylome through cell division with high fidelity (per-site error ~5%).

DNMT3A and DNMT3B are de novo methyltransferases that establish new patterns during embryogenesis and gametogenesis, working with the catalytically dead cofactor DNMT3L. They show partial substrate preference: DNMT3A targets euchromatin and is critical in haematopoietic stem cells (heterozygous DNMT3A R882H mutations are among the most common driver mutations in AML), while DNMT3B targets pericentric satellites and minor satellites; loss-of-function causes ICF syndrome (immunodeficiency, centromeric instability, facial anomalies).

Targeting specificity is largely indirect. DNMT3A/B are recruited by H3K36me2/3 (via PWWP domains) and excluded from H3K4me3 (active promoters) by ADD-domain readout. Genetic loss of any one DNMT in mice is embryonic-lethal or perinatally lethal, underscoring methylation's essentiality in mammals.

concepts.title: Erasers: TET Enzymes and Active Demethylation
concepts.contentHtml:
Demethylation can occur passively — failure to maintain methylation through replication dilutes 5mC by half each division. Active demethylation is performed by the TET (ten-eleven translocation) family of α-ketoglutarate / Fe(II)-dependent dioxygenases, which iteratively oxidise 5mC → 5hmC → 5fC → 5caC. The oxidised bases 5fC and 5caC are excised by thymine DNA glycosylase (TDG) and replaced with unmodified C through base excision repair.

TET activity is exquisitely metabolism-coupled. The cofactor α-ketoglutarate is a TCA cycle intermediate; the oncometabolite 2-hydroxyglutarate (produced by mutant IDH1/2 in gliomas and AML) is a competitive inhibitor of TETs and KDM histone demethylases, producing the characteristic CpG-island methylator phenotype (G-CIMP) of IDH-mutant tumours.

5hmC is itself a stable mark, abundant in brain (~1% of cytosines in Purkinje neurons) and embryonic stem cells. Distinguishing 5mC from 5hmC requires specialised sequencing — oxBS-seq, TAB-seq, or enzymatic methods such as EM-seq — because standard bisulfite conversion reads both as C.
mathExpressions: P(\text{5mC}_{\text{daughter}} \mid \text{5mC}_{\text{parent}}) \approx 0.95 \quad \text{(DNMT1 maintenance fidelity per CpG per cell division)}

title: The Histone Code
description: Writers, readers, erasers, and the combinatorial logic of histone modifications

concepts.title: Modification Types and Their Locations
concepts.contentHtml:
Histone tails — the unstructured N-terminal extensions protruding from the nucleosome core — accept dozens of post-translational modifications. The major classes are methylation (mono-, di-, tri- on lysines and arginines), acetylation (lysines), phosphorylation (serine/threonine), ubiquitination (lysines), and SUMOylation. Each has positional logic.

Canonical active marks: H3K4me3 at active promoters (placed by MLL/SET1), H3K4me1 + H3K27ac at active enhancers (MLL3/4 and p300/CBP), H3K36me3 across actively transcribed gene bodies (SETD2, co-transcriptional via RNAPII Ser2P), and pan-acetylation (H3K9ac, H3K14ac, H4K16ac) reducing positive charge to relax chromatin.

Canonical repressive marks: H3K9me2/3 for constitutive heterochromatin (SUV39H1/2, SETDB1; bound by HP1), H3K27me3 for facultative repression (deposited by Polycomb Repressive Complex 2 — EZH2 catalytic subunit, with EED and SUZ12), and H2AK119ub1 deposited by PRC1's RING1A/B. H3K9me3 and H3K27me3 are mechanistically and developmentally distinct: knocking out PRC2 derepresses HOX clusters; knocking out SUV39H derepresses pericentric satellites.

concepts.title: Writers, Readers, Erasers
concepts.contentHtml:
Three enzyme classes operate the code. Writers add modifications: KMTs (lysine methyltransferases) such as EZH2, MLL1, SUV39H1; KATs (lysine acetyltransferases) such as p300/CBP, GCN5, MOF. Erasers remove them: KDMs (lysine demethylases) split into FAD-dependent LSD1/KDM1 and the JmjC family (KDM2–7); HDACs (histone deacetylases) class I (HDAC1–3, 8), class IIa/b (HDAC4–7, 9, 10), class III (sirtuins SIRT1–7, NAD+-dependent).

Readers bind specific modifications via dedicated domains: chromodomains read methyl-lysines (HP1 reads H3K9me3, Polycomb CBX reads H3K27me3), PHD fingers read H3K4me3 (TAF3, BPTF) or unmodified H3K4 (BHC80), bromodomains read acetyl-lysines (BRD4 reads H4K16ac at super-enhancers; the BET inhibitor JQ1 displaces it), Tudor domains read methylated arginines, and 14-3-3 reads phospho-serines.

The reader is what gives the modification meaning. H3K27me3 is silencing because CBX-PRC1 binds it and ubiquitinates H2AK119; the mark itself does nothing without the reader. Drugging the reader (BET inhibitors, EED inhibitors of PRC2 read-write feedback) is therapeutically more tractable than drugging the catalysis.

concepts.title: Bivalent Domains and Combinatorial Logic
concepts.contentHtml:
The original histone code hypothesis (Strahl & Allis, 2000; Jenuwein & Allis, 2001) proposed that combinations of marks specify transcriptional outputs more richly than any single mark. The clearest example is the bivalent domain in embryonic stem cells: lineage-specifying genes such as HOX, SOX, and PAX carry both activating H3K4me3 and repressing H3K27me3 simultaneously (Bernstein et al., 2006). The gene is poised — silent but ready to resolve in either direction during differentiation.

Other combinatorial logic: H3K4me1 alone marks primed enhancers; adding H3K27ac activates them; adding H3K27me3 instead poises them. Super-enhancers are dense clusters of H3K4me1/H3K27ac spanning >10 kb, bound by Mediator and BRD4, and they drive cell-identity genes with disproportionate sensitivity to perturbation.

Cross-talk between marks is enzymatically encoded. H3S10ph (mitotic) ejects HP1 from H3K9me3 via a phospho-methyl switch. PRC2's EED subunit reads H3K27me3 and allosterically activates EZH2's catalysis on neighbouring nucleosomes, producing the read–write feedback that lets H3K27me3 spread and stably propagate.

title: Non-Coding RNA
description: miRNA, lncRNA, piRNA, circRNA, and the regulatory RNA universe

concepts.title: miRNAs: Seed Pairing and the RISC
concepts.contentHtml:
microRNAs are ~22 nt RNAs that post-transcriptionally repress mRNAs. Biogenesis: a primary transcript (pri-miRNA) is cleaved in the nucleus by the Drosha/DGCR8 Microprocessor into a ~70 nt hairpin pre-miRNA, exported by Exportin-5, and processed in the cytoplasm by Dicer with TRBP into the mature duplex. One strand (the guide) loads into Argonaute (typically AGO2 in mammals) to form the RISC; the passenger strand is discarded.

Target recognition is dominated by the seed sequence: nucleotides 2–8 of the miRNA must Watson–Crick pair with the 3' UTR of the mRNA. Seed matches as short as 6 nt are functional; 7- and 8-mer matches with adenine flanking are most potent. A single miRNA typically has hundreds of targets, and a single mRNA can be regulated by many miRNAs combinatorially.

The repression mechanism in animals is mostly mRNA destabilisation: AGO recruits the CCR4-NOT deadenylase via TNRC6/GW182, deadenylates the poly-A tail, and triggers decapping and exonucleolytic decay. Translational inhibition contributes more transiently. miRNAs are essential — global Dicer knockout is embryonic-lethal — and many (let-7, miR-17~92, miR-21) are oncogenes or tumour suppressors.

concepts.title: Long Non-Coding RNAs
concepts.contentHtml:
lncRNAs are RNAs longer than 200 nt without coding potential. The human genome encodes ~16,000 of them (GENCODE). Most are RNAPII transcripts, capped, spliced, and polyadenylated, often expressed at low abundance and with high tissue specificity. Their mechanisms are remarkably diverse.

Scaffold: HOTAIR (transcribed from the HOXC locus) binds PRC2 at one end and LSD1/CoREST at the other, targeting both complexes to repress HOXD in trans. Decoy: GAS5 mimics a glucocorticoid response element and titrates the GR away from chromatin. Guide: XIST recruits silencing complexes in cis on the X chromosome (covered later). Enhancer-like: HOTTIP activates HOXA genes via chromosomal looping.

Some lncRNAs work co-transcriptionally — the act of transcribing them, rather than the RNA product itself, is what matters. The classic example is Airn, whose transcription across the Igf2r promoter sterically displaces RNAPII. lncRNA function is contested for many candidates: of the ~16,000 annotated lncRNAs, only a few hundred have well-validated mechanisms, and CRISPR-screen studies suggest many are functionally inert transcriptional noise.

concepts.title: piRNAs and circRNAs
concepts.contentHtml:
piRNAs (PIWI-interacting RNAs) are 24–32 nt RNAs that protect germline genome integrity by silencing transposable elements. They differ from miRNAs in that biogenesis is Dicer-independent — primary piRNAs come from long single-stranded precursors transcribed from piRNA clusters (e.g., flamenco in Drosophila, the Pi6/Pi17 clusters in mouse). The ping-pong cycle amplifies piRNAs against active transposons: Aub-bound antisense piRNA cleaves a sense transposon transcript, generating a sense piRNA that loads into Ago3 and cleaves antisense cluster transcripts in turn. Loss of piRNAs causes transposon derepression and complete sterility.

Circular RNAs are formed by back-splicing: a downstream 5' splice site joins to an upstream 3' splice site, producing a covalently closed loop with no 5' cap or 3' poly-A tail. The reaction is favoured when reverse-complementary Alu repeats flank the back-spliced exon, base-pairing the introns into proximity (Jeck et al., 2013).

Functions remain partially mysterious. CDR1as / ciRS-7 is the canonical example: it carries ~70 binding sites for miR-7 and acts as a miRNA sponge, raising miR-7 targets when expressed. Most circRNAs are expressed at low stoichiometry relative to their host linear transcripts, so universal sponge activity is unlikely; many may simply be splicing byproducts that happen to be stable.

title: CRISPR-Cas Systems
description: Mechanism, gRNA design, off-targets, base editing, and prime editing

concepts.title: Natural CRISPR Systems and the Cas Zoo
concepts.contentHtml:
CRISPR-Cas is a prokaryotic adaptive immune system. Bacteria capture short fragments of invading phage DNA ("spacers") and integrate them into CRISPR arrays between repeat sequences, then transcribe and process them into crRNAs that guide Cas effector proteins to cleave matching foreign nucleic acid on subsequent infection.

Systems are classified by effector architecture. Class 1 uses multi-protein effector complexes: Type I (Cascade + Cas3, the most abundant in nature) destroys DNA processively. Type III (Csm/Cmr) targets RNA and DNA simultaneously and produces cyclic-oligoadenylate second messengers. Class 2 uses a single multi-domain effector — these are the engineering workhorses: Type II = Cas9 (DNA, dual-RNA: crRNA+tracrRNA), Type V = Cas12a/Cpf1 (DNA, single crRNA, staggered cuts), Type VI = Cas13 (RNA-targeting, used for diagnostics like SHERLOCK).

For genome editing, Streptococcus pyogenes Cas9 (SpCas9) became dominant after Jinek et al. (2012) fused crRNA + tracrRNA into a single sgRNA. Cas12a has advantages for multiplexing because it processes its own crRNA arrays. Compact orthologs (SaCas9, CasΦ) fit into single AAV vectors for in vivo delivery.

concepts.title: Guide Design, PAM, and Off-Targets
concepts.contentHtml:
SpCas9 targeting requires a PAM (protospacer adjacent motif) of NGG immediately 3' of the 20 nt protospacer. The PAM is read first by Cas9's PI domain; only then does the guide unwind the DNA and probe for complementarity, propagating an R-loop from the PAM-proximal seed (positions 1–10 from the PAM) outward. Mismatches in the PAM-proximal seed abolish cleavage; mismatches in the PAM-distal end (positions 11–20) are often tolerated.

This tolerance is the source of off-target editing. Empirical off-target profiling — GUIDE-seq, CIRCLE-seq, DISCOVER-seq — typically finds 1–100 off-target sites per guide. Mitigations: pick guides with high uniqueness scores (CFD, MIT score), use high-fidelity variants (eSpCas9, SpCas9-HF1, HiFi-Cas9), use paired nickases (D10A nickase + two offset guides — both must hit for a DSB), or use ribonucleoprotein delivery for transient activity.

PAM expansion engineering — SpG (NGN), SpRY (NRN/NYN essentially PAMless), xCas9, NG-Cas9 — has dramatically increased the targetable fraction of the genome, at some cost in efficiency and specificity. Choosing the right Cas variant, guide, and delivery format is now a domain of its own.

concepts.title: Base Editing and Prime Editing
concepts.contentHtml:
Cleaving DNA and relying on HDR (homology-directed repair) for precise edits is inefficient outside dividing cells, and NHEJ mostly produces indels. Two breakthroughs avoid the DSB. Base editors (Komor et al., 2016; Gaudelli et al., 2017) fuse a catalytically impaired Cas9 (nickase or dead) to a deaminase. Cytosine base editors (CBE) use a cytidine deaminase (APOBEC1, evoAPOBEC, etc.) to convert C → U → T within a ~5 nt activity window, enabling C·G → T·A transitions. Adenine base editors (ABE) use an evolved tRNA adenosine deaminase (TadA) for A → I → G, giving A·T → G·C. Together CBE+ABE access all four transition mutations.

Prime editing (Anzalone et al., 2019) extends scope to all 12 substitutions plus small indels. The PE2 protein is Cas9 H840A nickase fused to an engineered M-MLV reverse transcriptase. The pegRNA contains the guide plus a 3' extension specifying the desired edit and a primer-binding site. After nicking, the released 3' end primes RT extension on the pegRNA template, writing the edit directly into the genome. PE3 adds a second nick on the opposite strand to bias resolution toward the edit.

Trade-offs: base editors are more efficient but are bystander-edit-prone and limited to transitions; prime editing is more precise and flexible but less efficient (typically 1–30% in primary cells). The first in vivo base-editing therapy (Verve VERVE-101 for PCSK9, 2023) and the first prime-editing trials are now in clinic.

title: Gene Regulatory Networks
description: Transcription factors, enhancers, motifs, and network motifs

concepts.title: Transcription Factors and Sequence Motifs
concepts.contentHtml:
The human genome encodes ~1,600 transcription factors. They bind DNA via structured domains: zinc fingers (~700 in humans, the largest class — including KRAB-ZFPs that target endogenous retroviruses), homeodomains (HOX, PAX, OTX), basic helix-loop-helix (MYC, MYOD, HIF), basic leucine zipper (FOS, JUN, ATF, CREB), and nuclear receptors (ER, AR, GR with their hormone-binding LBD).

Each TF recognises a degenerate motif typically 6–12 bp. Motifs are formalised as position weight matrices (PWMs): at each position, log-odds scores for each base relative to background. Resources like JASPAR and HOCOMOCO catalogue PWMs derived from ChIP-seq and SELEX data. The information content of a PWM, in bits, indicates how rare the motif is by chance.

A canonical motif occurs by chance every 4^L / I bp (where L is motif length and I is its information content). For a 10-bp motif at full information, that's once per million bp — but most TFs bind only a tiny subset of their motif occurrences. Real binding is shaped by chromatin accessibility, cooperative binding, and DNA shape readout (minor groove width, propeller twist), not just sequence.
mathExpressions: I(\text{motif}) = \sum_{i=1}^{L} \sum_{b \in \{A,C,G,T\}} f_{i,b} \log_2 \frac{f_{i,b}}{p_b} \quad \text{(motif information content in bits)}

concepts.title: Enhancers and Super-Enhancers
concepts.contentHtml:
Enhancers are distal cis-regulatory elements that increase transcription of target promoters, often hundreds of kilobases away, in an orientation- and position-independent manner. They are characterised by H3K4me1 + H3K27ac, DNase/ATAC accessibility, and bidirectional eRNA transcription. The mammalian genome contains ~10⁵–10⁶ candidate enhancers — far outnumbering genes — and each gene is regulated by an average of 5–10.

Enhancer–promoter contact occurs through chromatin looping, mostly within TADs. The mediator complex and BRD4 bridge enhancer-bound TFs to promoter-bound RNAPII; cohesin and CTCF organise the topology. The looping is increasingly modelled as a transcriptional condensate formed by IDRs of TFs, Mediator, and BRD4 that phase-separate and concentrate the transcription machinery.

Super-enhancers (Whyte et al., 2013) are exceptionally large clusters (>10 kb) with extreme density of TF and Mediator binding. They are typically <5% of enhancers but drive the most cell-identity-defining genes, and they are disproportionately sensitive to BRD4 inhibition (the basis for BET inhibitors like JQ1 in MYC-driven cancers). MYC, OCT4, NANOG, KLF4 all loop to super-enhancers in their respective lineages.

concepts.title: Network Motifs and Dynamical Logic
concepts.contentHtml:
Gene regulatory networks are graphs: nodes are TFs and their targets, edges are activation or repression. Within these graphs, certain small subgraphs — network motifs — appear far more often than in randomised controls (Alon, Milo, et al., 2002). They implement specific computational functions.

The feed-forward loop (FFL): TF X regulates Y, and both X and Y regulate Z. The coherent type-1 FFL (X→Y→Z and X→Z, both activations, AND-logic) acts as a delay filter — it ignores brief X pulses and only responds to sustained signal. The incoherent type-1 FFL generates a pulse — Z rises with X, then falls as Y catches up and represses. Both are abundant in E. coli and yeast.

Negative autoregulation speeds up response time and reduces noise — appearing in ~40% of E. coli TFs. Positive autoregulation with cooperative binding creates bistable switches, the basis of cell-fate decisions (e.g., the lambda phage lysis–lysogeny switch, the GATA1/PU.1 erythroid–myeloid switch in haematopoiesis). Single-cell measurements have validated these dynamics quantitatively, transforming network biology from descriptive cataloguing into predictive dynamical modelling.

title: Genomic Imprinting and X-Inactivation
description: Parent-of-origin effects, imprinting control regions, and dosage compensation

concepts.title: Genomic Imprinting and Parent-of-Origin Effects
concepts.contentHtml:
Genomic imprinting is the parent-of-origin-dependent monoallelic expression of a small subset of mammalian genes — about 150 in humans. The two parental alleles are genetically identical at imprinted loci but differ epigenetically, so one is silent and the other expressed.

The mechanism centres on imprinting control regions (ICRs) — differentially methylated regions established in the germline. During spermatogenesis or oogenesis, sex-specific methylation is laid down on ICRs by DNMT3A/L. After fertilisation, ICRs are protected from the global demethylation wave that erases other methylation marks, by ZFP57/KAP1 reading the methylated TGCCGC motif at ICRs and recruiting maintenance methylation machinery.

The Igf2/H19 locus is the canonical example. The ICR is methylated on the paternal allele; CTCF cannot bind methylated DNA, so the paternal allele lets the downstream enhancer activate Igf2. On the maternal unmethylated allele, CTCF binds and forms an insulator that blocks the enhancer from Igf2, instead activating the lncRNA H19. Net result: paternal Igf2, maternal H19, both monoallelic from the same locus.

concepts.title: Prader-Willi vs Angelman: Same Deletion, Different Disease
concepts.contentHtml:
The 15q11-q13 imprinted cluster contains several paternally expressed genes (SNRPN, NDN, MAGEL2, the SNORD116 snoRNA cluster) and one maternally expressed gene (UBE3A, expressed maternally only in neurons). A loss of the paternal 15q11-q13 — by deletion (~70%), maternal uniparental disomy (~25%), or imprinting-centre defect — causes Prader-Willi syndrome: hypotonia, hyperphagia, obesity, hypogonadism, intellectual disability. Loss of the maternal 15q11-q13 causes Angelman syndrome: severe intellectual disability, ataxia, seizures, frequent laughter — primarily from loss of neuronal UBE3A.

The same chromosomal deletion produces two profoundly different diseases depending on which parent it came from. This is the cleanest demonstration that imprinting is functionally consequential, not curious trivia.

Therapeutically, UBE3A on the paternal allele is silenced by an antisense lncRNA (UBE3A-ATS). Antisense oligonucleotides that block UBE3A-ATS reactivate paternal UBE3A in neurons; this strategy is now in clinical trials for Angelman syndrome and is one of the most promising epigenetic therapies in development.

concepts.title: X-Inactivation: Xist, Choice, and Escapees
concepts.contentHtml:
Female mammals silence one of two X chromosomes to equalise X-linked dosage with XY males — X-chromosome inactivation (XCI). Initiation depends on the X-inactivation centre (Xic), in particular the lncRNA Xist. Xist is transcribed from the future inactive X (Xi), coats it in cis, and recruits silencing machinery: SPEN to recruit HDAC3, SAF-A/HNRNPU to anchor Xist on chromatin, and Polycomb (via hnRNPK→PRC1→PRC2 read-write) to deposit H2AK119ub and H3K27me3 across the chromosome.

Choice of which X to inactivate is stochastic and clonally inherited. Xist on the future-Xi is upregulated; its antisense lncRNA Tsix represses Xist on the future-Xa. Once committed, the Xa is locked active by DNA methylation of the Xist promoter on Xa. After establishment, XCI maintenance becomes Xist-independent — re-expressing Xist in adult cells only modestly perturbs silencing.

Roughly 15–25% of human X-linked genes escape inactivation, expressed from both alleles. Escapees cluster in the pseudoautosomal regions and explain why Turner syndrome (45,X) is viable while monosomies of autosomes are not: half-dosage of escapees (SHOX, USP9X, KDM6A) drives the Turner phenotype. Skewed XCI — where one X is preferentially inactivated >80:20 — can mask or unmask X-linked recessive disease in heterozygous females, producing carrier females with disease (DMD, Fabry, hemophilia) and the classical mosaic phenotype of calico cats.

title: Transgenerational Epigenetic Inheritance
description: Resetting, evidence, controversies, and the Dutch Hunger Winter

concepts.title: Two Waves of Reprogramming
concepts.contentHtml:
The mammalian germline and early embryo undergo two near-complete epigenetic reprogramming events that erase most parental epigenetic information. The first occurs in primordial germ cells (PGCs) migrating to the gonadal ridge: between E8.5 and E13.5 in mouse, PGCs lose nearly all DNA methylation, including at most imprinting control regions, dropping from ~70% to <5% genome-wide. New sex-specific imprints are then established during gametogenesis.

The second wave occurs after fertilisation. The paternal pronucleus is rapidly demethylated by TET3-mediated 5mC→5hmC oxidation; the maternal pronucleus is demethylated more passively through replication. Total methylation reaches its nadir at the blastocyst's inner cell mass, and is re-established lineage-specifically during gastrulation by DNMT3A/B.

Imprinting control regions, certain repetitive elements (IAPs, LINE-1s), and a small set of "escape" loci resist reprogramming. The protection is largely mediated by ZFP57 and TRIM28 reading methylated motifs and recruiting maintenance machinery. These resistant loci are the only mechanistically plausible carriers of stable transgenerational epigenetic information in mammals — and even at IAPs the resistance is incomplete.

concepts.title: Evidence and Controversies
concepts.contentHtml:
Strict transgenerational epigenetic inheritance requires that an environmentally induced epigenetic state pass through the germline and persist in unexposed descendants beyond the F2 generation in maternal exposure (the F0 mother, F1 fetus, and F2 germline are all directly exposed) or beyond F1 in paternal exposure. Most claimed examples in mammals are confounded by direct in-utero exposure or by genetic effects.

The strongest mammalian models. Agouti viable yellow (Avy) mice carry an IAP retrotransposon upstream of agouti; methylation of the IAP varies stochastically, producing a coat-colour spectrum from yellow (low methylation) to agouti (high). Maternal diet (folate, methyl donors, BPA) shifts offspring methylation and coat colour, and the methylation state is partly inherited matrilineally for one or two further generations.

In C. elegans, RNAi-induced silencing via the WAGO/HRDE-1 pathway can persist for 3–80+ generations through germline 22G-RNAs and H3K9me3 — the cleanest example of transgenerational epigenetic inheritance in any animal, though worms lack DNA methylation. In plants, hypomethylated epialleles at colorless non-ripening in tomato or Lcyc in Linaria are stable for many generations, because plants lack the embryonic reprogramming wave seen in mammals.

concepts.title: The Dutch Hunger Winter and DOHaD
concepts.contentHtml:
The Dutch Hunger Winter (Hongerwinter, 1944–45) imposed a sudden severe famine on western Netherlands. The population's medical records have made it a natural experiment for developmental origins of health and disease (DOHaD). Adults exposed in early gestation showed persistent hypomethylation at the IGF2 imprinted locus six decades later (Heijmans et al., 2008), with elevated rates of obesity, type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and schizophrenia. Mid- and late-gestation exposure produced different metabolic phenotypes — early-gestation exposure was the worst.

Other cohorts (the Överkalix Swedish cohort linking grandfather food supply at age 9–12 to grandson cardiovascular mortality; the ALSPAC, Avon, and ENRICH cohorts) report associations between ancestral exposures and descendant phenotypes.

The interpretation is contested. Direct in-utero exposure (F1 fetus, F2 germ cells) trivially explains effects through F2; genuinely transgenerational effects through F3 in mammals are not robustly established. Paternal contributions via sperm tRNA fragments and miRNAs (Chen et al., 2016; Rando lab) are mechanistically plausible but contested for magnitude. The honest position is: real molecular mechanisms exist (sperm small-RNA payloads, IAP methylation states, paternal histone retention), demonstrated effects on F1–F2 phenotypes are real, and claims of effects beyond F3 in mammals require extraordinary evidence and usually do not survive replication.

title: Single-Cell Epigenomics
description: scATAC-seq, scRNA-seq, scBS-seq, and the multi-omic integration problem

concepts.title: scRNA-seq and scATAC-seq
concepts.contentHtml:
Single-cell RNA-seq profiles the transcriptome of individual cells. The dominant platform, 10x Genomics Chromium, uses droplet microfluidics to co-encapsulate each cell with a barcoded gel bead; reverse transcription inside the droplet tags every cDNA with the cell barcode and a unique molecular identifier (UMI) that distinguishes original transcripts from PCR duplicates. A typical experiment yields 5,000–20,000 cells per channel at ~50,000 reads/cell, capturing ~2,000–5,000 genes per cell.

The data are extremely sparse — most genes register zero counts in most cells ("dropout"). Analysis pipelines (Scanpy, Seurat) normalise, identify highly variable genes, run PCA, then non-linear embedding (UMAP, t-SNE) and graph-based clustering (Leiden) to find cell types, plus pseudotime methods (Slingshot, Monocle3, RNA velocity) for trajectories.

scATAC-seq profiles chromatin accessibility per cell using Tn5 transposase, which simultaneously fragments and tags accessible DNA with sequencing adapters. Open regions yield reads; closed regions don't. Per-cell coverage is even sparser than scRNA-seq. Analysis identifies accessible peaks, scores TF motif activity (chromVAR), and links peaks to genes by co-accessibility (Cicero) or to nearby transcription via paired multi-omic assays.

concepts.title: scBS-seq, scNMT-seq, and Methylation at Single-Cell Resolution
concepts.contentHtml:
Single-cell bisulfite sequencing (scBS-seq) profiles DNA methylation per cell. Genomic DNA from individual cells is bisulfite-treated (unmethylated C deaminates to U, methylated C is protected) and sequenced. Coverage is brutally sparse: a single cell yields methylation calls at ~10–40% of CpGs, far too few for most analyses without pooling. Methods like Melissa, scMET, and HMM-based callers impute methylation states using shared structure across cells.

The HMM framework treats methylation along a CpG sequence as a hidden state Markov chain: P(state_i | state_{i-1}) captures the spatial autocorrelation, while P(read | state_i) models bisulfite conversion noise and PCR error. Forward-backward inference yields per-CpG posterior probabilities even at uncovered sites. Specialised methods like DeepSignal and Megalodon achieve direct methylation calling from nanopore current signal without bisulfite, and approach single-cell resolution at long-read throughput.

Multi-modal assays combine layers in the same cell. scNMT-seq (Clark et al., 2018) profiles transcriptome, DNA methylation, and chromatin accessibility (via GpC methyltransferase footprinting) simultaneously. SHARE-seq and 10x Multiome jointly profile RNA + ATAC. CITE-seq adds surface protein. Joint analysis enables direct causal inference of how methylation or accessibility shifts predict transcriptional state.

concepts.title: Integration, Atlases, and Spatial Genomics
concepts.contentHtml:
The frontier is multi-modal integration: aligning scRNA-seq, scATAC-seq, scBS-seq, proteomics, and spatial assays into a unified cell-state representation. Methods like Seurat WNN, MOFA+, totalVI, and GLUE learn shared latent embeddings across modalities, often using variational autoencoders or canonical correlation analysis. The Human Cell Atlas, BRAIN Initiative Cell Census Network, and ENCODE Phase 4 are systematically applying these approaches at million-cell scale.

Spatial transcriptomics (Visium, Slide-seqV2, MERFISH, Stereo-seq) preserves tissue context. Visium uses an array of barcoded spots (~55 µm, several cells each); MERFISH uses combinatorial smFISH for true single-cell resolution at hundreds of genes; Stereo-seq achieves subcellular resolution at whole-genome scope. Spatial epigenomics is rapidly catching up — spatial-ATAC-seq and spatial-CUT&Tag (Deng et al., 2022) profile accessibility and histone marks with tissue context.

Open challenges: batch effects across labs and platforms, the identifiability problem in trajectory inference (multiple latent dynamics fit the same snapshot data), missing temporal resolution (snapshots vs lineage), and the gulf between cell-type and cell-state. Lineage-tracing barcodes (LARRY, GESTALT, Watermelon) and metabolic labelling (sci-fate, scEU-seq) are beginning to add the temporal axis. The eventual goal is a predictive model: input genotype + environment, output cell-type-specific transcriptome, methylome, and developmental trajectory.
